topic.title: Grammar Learning and Hierarchical Language Structure
topic.area: Language Models and Natural Language Processing
topic.overview: This topic studies how linguistic structure can be learned and represented, from probabilistic transducers to grammar induction and neural parsing. Local word statistics must support relationships that span larger phrases and nested constructions. Compact parameter sharing and contextual information help models generalize beyond memorized strings.
topic.whyItMatters: A system may predict nearby words accurately while failing to recover the hierarchical organization needed for compositional understanding. Tractable language models make it possible to test which statistics support that organization and how ambiguity affects learning.
topic.evolution: The historical examples include parallel parsers in the late 1980s and shared-context transducers in 1997. Later papers learn constituent and dependency structure. A recent controlled grammar study connects cross-scale correlations with the emergence of hierarchical neural representations. This provides a testable mechanism in a simplified setting, not a complete explanation of natural-language acquisition.
openQuestions: Which language statistics support hierarchy rather than surface pattern matching?
How do findings from controlled grammars transfer to noisy, heterogeneous natural text?
